t: Count Artifacts That Can Be Extracted
o: Each artifact occupies a small rectangle (≤4 cells). A dig set tells us which cells are excavated; an artifact is extractable iff every cell of its rectangle was dug. Walk through Example 1: artifact [0,0,0,0] needs only cell (0,0), which is dug → extractable. Artifact [0,1,1,1] needs cells (0,1),(1,1); (1,1) wasn't dug → not extractable. Answer: 1. In Example 2 all needed cells are dug, so both count. Constraints allow up to 10^5 digs and artifacts, so we need roughly O(n^2 + artifacts + dig) work — anything per-dig scanning all artifacts would be too slow.
k: Map every dug cell to the artifact covering it using an n×n grid of artifact indices.
Count remaining undug cells per artifact; extractable when that counter hits zero.
Total work is bounded by grid size plus input size, comfortably within limits.

a.i: Build an n×n array storing which artifact index covers each cell. For each dig, decrement the covered artifact's remaining-cell counter. An artifact is extracted exactly when its counter reaches 0.
s: Create grid[n][n] initialized to -1 and rem[i] = number of cells in artifact i.
Fill grid[r][c] = i for every cell of artifact i.
For each dig (r,c), if grid[r][c] >= 0, decrement rem[grid[r][c]].
a.t: O(n² + total artifact cells + |dig|) — building the grid dominates.

a.n: Approach 2: Hash set of dug cells
a.i: Instead of a full grid, store all dug coordinates in a hash set. Then for each artifact, enumerate its ≤4 cells and check membership directly. This avoids O(n²) memory when n is large relative to input.
s: Insert every dug (r,c) into a hash set encoded as r*n+c or a string key.
For each artifact, iterate over its rectangle's cells.
If any cell is missing from the set, skip; otherwise increment the answer.
a.t: O(|dig| + total artifact cells) — each artifact has at most 4 cells.

w: Prefer Approach 2 in interviews: it's simpler and uses memory proportional to input rather than the grid. Pitfalls: encoding cell keys correctly (use r*n+c to avoid collisions), remembering rectangles can be up to 4 cells so direct enumeration is safe. Follow-ups: what if artifacts could be arbitrarily large? Then the counting approach (decrement per dig) generalizes better since checking whole rectangles per dig becomes expensive.
